A gas turbine needs extensive cooling because its combustion process is continuous. Nearly all cooling air must pass through the inside of the engine.

15:1Ideal air/fuel ratio in the supplied material
>2,200°CTemperature could rise beyond this without surplus air
800–1,150°CHot-section range achieved through cooling
Turbine areaThe hottest area is in and around the turbines.
Continuous combustion
Very high internal heat
Air added beyond the ideal ratio
Hot-section temperature reduced
Key PointA large portion of the air entering the engine supports cooling rather than combustion.
Compare with reciprocating-engine cooling
Comparison of cooling context in reciprocating and gas turbine engines
Engine typeCombustion patternCooling method stated in the source
Reciprocating engineCombustion occurs every fourth stroke in a four-stroke engineAir over cylinder fins or liquid coolant through cylinder jackets
Gas turbine engineCombustion is continuousNearly all cooling air passes through the inside of the engine.
Additional source detail
The external case is much cooler than the interior, but heat conducted through metal makes the turbine-case area particularly hot at the outside skin.
Quick Recall: Why is turbine-engine cooling more demanding?
Because combustion is continuous, producing sustained high temperatures that require a large surplus of cooling air.
1 of 8

The engine uses an intricate internal air system to route ram and/or compressor bleed air to components deep inside the core.

  • Compressor cooling
  • Combustion chamber cooling
  • Turbine disc cooling
  • Turbine NGV and blade cooling
  • Accessory section cooling
Combustion liner

Film cooling

The liner induces a thin, fast-moving film of air over both its inner and outer surfaces.

Gas dilution

Before the turbine

Relatively cool air mixes with burned gases aft of the burners, reducing gas temperature before turbine entry.

Additional source detail
Can-annular burners may use a centre tube to carry cooling air into the burner centre, helping combustion efficiency and rapid gas dilution while minimising pressure losses.
Quick Recall: How are combustion chamber liners protected?
A thin, fast-moving film of secondary air passes over both the inner and outer liner surfaces.
2 of 8

The turbine area is the hottest part of the engine, so its discs, vanes, blades, and supporting bearings need direct cooling.

Turbine hardware

Disc, NGVs and blades

Secondary compressor air is routed to these components to limit heat exposure.

Critical lubrication point

Exhaust turbine bearing

It is identified as the most critical lubricating point because of the normally high temperature.

Combined cooling

Air + oil

Some engines use air cooling in addition to oil cooling for the turbine-support bearing.

Additional source detail
Cooling-air inlets may be provided around the engine exterior to admit air for the turbine case, bearings, and turbine nozzle. Internal air vented to components is ultimately ejected into the exhaust stream.
Quick Recall: Why is the exhaust turbine bearing especially important?
It is the most critical lubricating point because it operates in a normally high-temperature area.
3 of 8

Fireproof bulkheads and seals isolate the powerplant into zones. Calibrated airflow keeps temperatures acceptable and prevents harmful vapour buildup.

Zone 1

Fan case compartment

  • Contains the accessory case and EEC.
  • Ram air enters through the nose cowl.
  • Air exits through a louvered right-fan-cowl vent.
  • A relief door opens if pressure exceeds its limit.
Zone 2

Intermediate compressor case

  • Fan air enters from the upper fan duct.
  • Air returns to the fan stream at the lower end.
  • Ventilation is important because fuel and oil lines are present.
Zone 3

Core engine compartment

  • Extends from the high-pressure compressor to turbine cases.
  • Contains fuel/oil lines and accessories.
  • Air enters from the precooler exhaust and other areas.
RememberZone airflow performs two jobs: temperature control and ventilation to prevent harmful vapour accumulation.
Quick Recall: Which zone contains the accessory case and EEC?
Zone 1, around the fan case.
4 of 8

Supplying secondary air is another compressor function. Small ports in the compressor case allow air to be tapped from the stage that provides the required pressure or temperature.

Port selection

Stage depends on the job

Different compressor stages offer different pressures. The required pressure or temperature determines the bleed-port location.

Highest stage

Maximum pressure and temperature

Air is often taken from the final or highest-pressure stage because both pressure and temperature are at their maximum there.

Common DistinctionCooling air may be bled from early compressor stages, while air for other aircraft services may be selected from different stages and is often taken from the highest-pressure stage.
External services supplied by engine bleed air
External bleed-air servicePurpose stated in the material
Cabin systemPressurisation, heating, and cooling
Ice protectionDeicing and anti-icing equipment
Engine startingPneumatic starting of engines
Auxiliary drive unitsAir supply for ADUs
Additional source detail
High-pressure bleed air may need cooling. For cabin pressurisation or other heat-sensitive uses, it is routed through an air-conditioning unit before entering the cabin.
Quick Recall: What determines which compressor stage supplies bleed air?
The pressure or temperature required for the particular job.
5 of 8

Ice on the inlet duct or inlet guide vanes can disturb compressor airflow, reduce efficiency, and break off into the compressor, where it may damage blades.

Ground operation

Icing can occur up to 5°C

The source links this to the chilling effect of high inlet velocities, especially during high-speed engine operation on the ground.

Flight operation

Visible moisture

In flight, the supplied material states that anti-icing is selected when visible moisture is present as clouds or precipitation.

Anti-icing selected
Bleed valve opens
Hot air heats inlet components
Air exits through cowl grill
Quick Recall: Which inlet parts receive hot anti-icing air?
The inlet leading edge, nose dome, and inlet guide vanes.
6 of 8

Compressor air pressurises the bearing chamber seal. Because air pressure is greater than oil pressure, air moves inward through the seal and prevents oil leakage outward.

Seal principleAir pressure > Oil pressure
Therefore, air enters the chamber through the seal instead of allowing oil to escape.
Additional source detail
The seal air is normally tapped from an intermediate compressor stage and carried through internal passages or external tubes.
Quick Recall: What pressure relationship prevents oil leakage?
Air pressure is greater than oil pressure, so air flows inward through the seal.
7 of 8

The nacelle covers the engine and divides the external area into zones. Ram or fan air moves around the engine to remove heat, fluid, and vapour.

Nacelle structure

Main parts listed

  • Inlet cowl
  • Fan cowls
  • Thrust reverser ducts
  • Exhaust duct
Fire protection

Hot and cold separation

Fire seals separate the forward cold section from the aft turbine hot section and prevent combustible fumes moving aft to ignite on the engine case.

Four external-cooling purposesRemove heat · protect the nacelle · clear fluids and vapours · reduce fire hazard.
Additional source detail
When the engine is mounted on the aircraft side, outside air may flow around the case. Fan air is also passed around the engine exterior and nacelle.
Quick Recall: What do case drains do?
They discharge potential leaks overboard to prevent fluid buildup inside the nacelle.

Terms to Know — open only when needed
Bleed air
Air taken from a compressor stage through ports in the compressor case.
NGV
Turbine nozzle guide vane.
EEC
Electronic engine control, located in the Zone 1 fan-case area in the supplied example.
ADU
Auxiliary drive unit, listed as an external bleed-air service.
Nacelle
The engine covering that includes the inlet cowl, fan cowls, thrust reverser ducts, and exhaust duct.
Film cooling
A thin, fast-moving layer of air over the inner and outer surfaces of a combustion liner.
